definition.text: Load balancing distributes a set of tasks or incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online, so the overall work is processed more efficiently.

facts.text: Load balancing can improve response time and avoids overloading some nodes while others are left idle.
Busy websites must serve hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of concurrent requests, and the cost-effective way to meet that volume is to add more servers.
A load balancer sits in front of the servers and routes each request to one that can fulfil it, in a way that maximizes speed and capacity use, so no single server is overworked.
If a server goes down, the balancer redirects traffic to the remaining online servers; when a new server joins the group, requests start flowing to it automatically.
It enables horizontal scaling: additional servers are added to the pool and the balancer distributes traffic across all of them.
Beyond parallel computing, load balancing is widely used for HTTP requests on high-traffic sites, most commonly to provide one Internet service from many servers, sometimes known as a server farm.
A balancer's main jobs are traffic distribution, high availability, SSL termination, session persistence, scalability and health monitoring.
Which algorithm fits depends on the nature of the tasks, their complexity, the hardware and the error tolerance required, so a compromise must be found for each application.

title: Static and dynamic load balancing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Problem overview > Static and dynamic algorithms

definition.text: A load-balancing algorithm is static when it ignores the current state of the system and dynamic when it takes each node's current load into account.

facts.text: A static algorithm ignores system state such as processor load and relies on assumptions made beforehand about arrival times, resource needs and processor speeds.

Static algorithms are easy to set up and efficient for fairly regular tasks such as processing HTTP requests from a website, but statistical variance in assignment can still overload some computing units.
Dynamic algorithms use the current load of each node and can move tasks from an overloaded node to an underloaded one for faster processing.
Dynamic algorithms are much more complicated to design but can improve performance, particularly when execution time varies greatly from one task to another.
Dynamic algorithms need nodes to exchange information, and one that needs too much communication to reach its decisions risks slowing down the overall solution.
A dynamic architecture can be more modular because no specific node has to be dedicated to distributing the work.
The more is known about the tasks when deciding, the better the optimization; knowing the exact execution time of every task is an idealized and extremely rare situation.

notes: Anchor is the parent heading of the Static and Dynamic subsections.

title: Load balancing algorithms
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Scheduling algorithms

definition.text: Scheduling algorithms, also called load-balancing methods, are the rules a load balancer uses to decide which back-end server receives each request.

facts.text: Simple algorithms include random choice, round robin and least connections.

More sophisticated balancers may also weigh a server's reported load, response times, up/down status from a monitoring poll, active connections, geographic location, capabilities or recently assigned traffic.
Round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin and hash are static algorithms; least connections and least response time are dynamic ones.
Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest current connections to clients, factoring in each server's relative computing capacity; the method can also be weighted.

Least response time sends requests to the server selected by a formula combining the fastest response time and fewest active connections, and least bandwidth picks the server carrying the least traffic in Mbps.
Hashing applies a hash function to a key the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL, and routes by the result.
Random assignment of tasks to servers works quite well, and a random permutation computed in advance avoids per-assignment communication and the need for a distribution master.
Power of two choices picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

conflicts.text: Least connections is listed among the static load distribution methods.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia files it under 'Static load distribution without prior knowledge', but its own definition of static excludes methods that use system state; ByteByteGo lists it as dynamic.

notes: Wikipedia's Others list puts least connections under static methods, against its own static definition (c08acfe98f76); drafted as dynamic, consistent with the definition and ByteByteGo.

title: Round robin load balancing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Approaches > Static load distribution without prior knowledge > Round-robin scheduling

definition.text: Round robin sends each new request to the next server in sequence and starts again at the first server after the last.

facts.text: The first request goes to the first server, the next to the second, and so on down to the last, then the cycle restarts; the services are usually required to be stateless.
Weighted round robin lets the administrator give each server a weight, so more powerful servers handle more requests, to account for differing compute and traffic-handling capacity.
Sticky round robin improves on round robin: if a user's first request goes to service A, the following requests go to service A as well.
Lower-powered units may receive requests needing less computation or, when request sizes are homogeneous or unknown, simply fewer requests than larger units.

notes: More on the existing entry: the general round-robin scheduling page adds its fairness properties and weaknesses.

definition.text: A layer 4 load balancer routes on transport-level information such as IP addresses and ports, while a layer 7 load balancer reads whole requests and routes on their content.

facts.text: A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports, so it cannot perform content-based routing.
Layer 4 balancers are often dedicated hardware devices that can operate at high speed.
A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer, reads requests in their entirety and performs content-based routing, allowing load to be managed from a full understanding of the traffic.
Application-layer balancing comes in variations: host-based uses the requested hostname, path-based uses the entire URL, and content-based inspects the message, for example the value of a parameter.
Routing by URL needs plain HTTP, or HTTPS that is terminated (decrypted) at the balancer.
Platform-specific routing can send requests from different device types, such as mobiles and desktops, to specialized backend systems.

title: Hardware, software and cloud load balancers

definition.text: Load balancers come as physical hardware devices, as software on standard machines, or as managed cloud services.

facts.text: A hardware balancer is physical on-premises equipment that handles a large volume of traffic but often costs a lot, is fairly inflexible and runs proprietary firmware that needs maintenance and patches.
Software balancers are usually easier to deploy than hardware, cost-effective and flexible, and can be configured to the environment, at the cost of more set-up work.

Software balancers come as installable solutions needing configuration and management, or as a managed cloud service; cloud load balancers such as AWS Elastic Load Balancer are built into the provider's infrastructure.

title: DNS load balancing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Round-robin DNS

definition.text: DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to it are spread across a group of servers.

facts.text: Round-robin DNS associates several IP addresses with one domain name and hands them to clients in rotation, needing no dedicated software or hardware node.
Addresses are given a short expiration so the client is more likely to use a different IP next time; resolvers return the whole set, and servers may round-robin its order.
DNS load balancing has inherent limits: DNS does not check for server and network outages, and it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable.
In DNS delegation, a sub-domain such as www is delegated to a zone served by the website's own servers, each answering with its own address, so a down server simply does not respond.
With delegation the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the closest server, giving geo-sensitive balancing, and it works well for geographically spread servers.
A short TTL on the A-record diverts traffic quickly when a server fails, but individual clients may switch between servers in mid-session.

Returning multiple A or AAAA records and letting the client choose gives little control: records are picked randomly and each attracts roughly equal traffic, and SRV weights and priorities are not adopted for HTTP.

The authoritative server sees the recursive resolver's address, not the user's, so replies can be optimized only for the resolver; EDNS0 passes the client subnet, and anycast nameservers or network location maps steer to the closest datacenter.

title: Client-side load balancing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Client-side random load balancing

definition.text: In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection.

facts.text: The client is given a list of server IPs, delivered as a DNS list without round-robin or hardcoded, and randomly selects one on each connection.
It relies on all clients generating similar loads and on the law of large numbers to give a reasonably flat distribution across servers.
It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS caching servers skew round-robin DNS while random client selection is unaffected by caching.
A smart client that detects a down server and connects randomly again also provides fault tolerance.

title: Session persistence
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Persistence

definition.text: Session persistence, also called stickiness, sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

facts.text: Information kept across a user's session, if stored on one backend server, cannot be found when later requests go to other backends; for recomputable cached data this is only a performance issue.
Ideally the servers behind the balancer are not session-aware, usually by keeping sessions in a shared database or an in-memory store such as Memcached.
Sticky sessions send a user or device to the same resource to keep session state there; in sticky round robin, once a user's first request goes to service A, later ones do too.
The significant downside is no automatic failover: if the backend goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and sessions depending on it are lost.
Assignment can be based on username, client IP address or random choice; IP-based assignment may be unreliable because of DHCP, network address translation and web proxies.
Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, costing storage and possibly lost if it fails, and the client must keep state, which fails if a browser has disabled cookies.
Sophisticated balancers use multiple persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one method.

title: Session state storage
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Persistence

definition.text: Session state can be kept in a database, in the client's browser, or in a distributed hash table, so that the balancer is free to pick any backend server.

facts.text: Keeping per-session data in a database can reduce performance because it adds load to a database best used for less transient data; the database is often replicated and balanced to avoid a single point of failure.
When the client is a web browser, the data can live in the browser itself, through a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or through URL rewriting.

Client-side storage is generally preferred because the balancer can then pick any backend, but it may not suit complex business logic with large session state, and URL rewriting has major security issues.
Another option is to name each block of data and use a distributed hash table to assign that name pseudo-randomly to one of the available servers, which stores the block.

definition.text: A health check lets the load balancer tell whether a server is down or performing poorly so it can remove that server from the pool.

facts.text: The balancer polls servers for application-layer health and removes failed servers from the pool.
Components are monitored continually, for example web servers by fetching known pages; when one becomes unresponsive the balancer stops sending it traffic, and resumes when it is back online.
Continuous evaluation of instances directs requests only to those that are fully operational, which maintains performance and keeps service uninterrupted.

title: Load balancer failover

definition.text: Load balancing is often used to implement failover, the continuation of service after the failure of one or more components.

facts.text: The balancer is informed when a component fails and stops sending it traffic, then reroutes traffic to it when it returns.
For this to work there must be at least one component in excess of the service's capacity (N+1 redundancy).
This is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a backup that takes over on failure (dual modular redundancy).
Failover can raise fault tolerance by allowing quick substitution of the most complicated, failure-prone parts, but it can make the load balancer itself a single point of failure.
To avoid that, a second or N load balancers can run in cluster mode, and if the active one fails, a passive one takes over, making the system more fault-tolerant.
Balancers are usually implemented in high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it.
Some balancers do something special when all backend servers are unavailable, such as forwarding to a backup balancer or displaying a message about the outage.

notes: Includes the redundant-load-balancer practice (Singh 'Redundant load balancers' section, Wikipedia server-side balancers).

definition.text: A load balancer or reverse proxy can terminate TLS connections itself, decrypting traffic and passing plain requests to the backend servers so they are spared the encryption work.

facts.text: TLS encryption and authentication can become a major part of a web server's CPU demand; a balancer can terminate TLS and pass HTTPS requests to the web servers as HTTP.
Terminating TLS at the balancer lets it balance or switch content based on data inside the HTTPS request.
The downside is that all TLS processing is concentrated on one device, the balancer, which can become a new bottleneck; adding a few web servers may be cheaper than upgrading it.

The proxy must then decrypt and re-encrypt traffic it filters, caches or compresses, so it needs the TLS certificate and private key, widening access to unencrypted data and making it a more valuable attack target.

title: Load balancer features
article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Load balancer features

definition.text: Beyond distributing requests, load balancers offer a range of extra features, most of them vendor specific, such as compression, caching, security and connection handling.

facts.text: The fundamental feature is distributing incoming requests over the backend servers in the cluster according to a scheduling algorithm; most other features are vendor specific.

Asymmetric load assigns a manual ratio so some backends get a bigger share, a simple way to reflect capacity differences, and priority activation brings standby servers online when too few servers remain or load is too high.
Balancers can mitigate SYN flood attacks with features such as SYN cookies and delayed binding, where backends do not see the client until it completes its TCP handshake.
HTTP compression cuts transferred data and helps more for larger responses and distant clients, but adds CPU demand on the balancer and could be done by the web servers instead.

Connection multiplexing consolidates multiple HTTP requests from multiple clients into a single TCP socket to the backends, and TCP buffering spoon-feeds responses to slow clients so web server threads are freed sooner.
An application-layer balancer may cache static content to answer some requests without contacting the servers.
HTTP security features include hiding error pages, removing server identification headers and encrypting cookies so end users cannot manipulate them.
Logging request and response metadata gives an audit trail or analytics data, and request tracing gives each request a unique id for logging, monitoring and troubleshooting.

definition.text: Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve redundancy and performance at a global scale.

facts.text: It spreads traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve redundancy and performance on a global scale.
Cross-zone load balancing distributes incoming traffic across geographic or network zones, increasing the system's resilience and capacity for large volumes of requests.
Server-load balancing for content delivery uses service-based (global load balancing) or hardware-based techniques, such as layer 4-7 switches, to share traffic among several servers or web caches.
DNS-based delegation gives geo-sensitive balancing, since the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the network's closest server.

definition.text: In a master-worker scheme, a master hands out tasks to workers that ask for them, making it one of the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms.

facts.text: All workers start idle and report to the master, which answers their requests with tasks and tells them to stop asking when no tasks remain.
The scheme can distribute work evenly when the assignment overhead is low.
It scales badly to many processors because of the high amount of communication, and the master acts as a bottleneck.
Replacing the master with a task list shared by the processors improves it and scalability, though it is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

title: Work stealing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Approaches > Non-hierarchical architecture, without knowledge of the system: work stealing

definition.text: Work stealing gives each processor some tasks, then lets idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones.

facts.text: It overcomes scalability problems when task completion time is unknown: tasks are assigned randomly or in a predefined way, then inactive processors steal work from active or overloaded ones.
An idle processor requests work at random from others; if the target can subdivide its task it sends part of it, otherwise it returns an empty task.
It can be particularly effective but is difficult to implement, since communication must not become the processors' primary occupation instead of solving the problem.
Its efficiency is close to the optimal prefix-sum distribution when the cost of splitting jobs and communicating is not too high compared with the work.
